Phoenix, Arizona · ride

Bike routes in Phoenix

The rides locals in Phoenix actually do, each with a route you can load.

Best months: November to April.

More on when to ride

Summer highs average 104 to 106 F. On Extreme Heat Warning days the city closes named preserve trails from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; in 2026 those closures began March 19. From May to October, ride at first light and carry all your water.

Bike routes in Phoenix, listed

What do you need?

  1. South Mountain, Summit Road to the towers

    The city’s climb: Summit Road from the ranger station to the radio towers at the top.

    • Climb
    • 7 mi
    • 1,330 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: The ranger station at the bottom of Summit Road, South Mountain Park/Preserve
    • Water: A water fountain, restrooms and a vending machine at the ranger station at the start (PJAMM); nothing on the climb.
    • Watch: PJAMM: minimal shoulder most of the way, blind corners with nowhere to bail out on the descent, and a hole or two to watch for on the way down.

    Ride it with the group: Silent Sunday at South Mountain (Sundays, 5:00 am) →

    Route pageTo the start
    More about South Mountain, Summit Road to the towers

    PJAMM measures 7 miles and 1,330 feet at 3.2 percent. The road dips on the way up; without those bits it is 4.8 percent, and the steepest quarter-mile is 8.9 percent. Dobbins Lookout, at 2,330 feet, is the highest point in the park open to the public (City of Phoenix). Every Sunday, cars are stopped at the 1.0 mile marker from 5 to 10 a.m. On the 4th Sunday of the month the road is closed to cars all day, 5 a.m. to 7 p.m., and drivers park at the Activity Complex. The park’s entrance and parking hours are 5 a.m. to 7 p.m. Valley Epic Rides’ Taco Tuesday group rides the park’s trails from Ahwatukee, on the far side of the mountain.

    Surface: Paved park road. PJAMM calls it adequate and says it is cracked in many places from heat.

    Watch: Outside the Silent Sunday hours cars use the road; PJAMM calls traffic minimal. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). On Extreme Heat Warning days the city closes the Holbert, Mormon and Hau’pal Loop trails, and the National Trail from Pima Canyon, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The list does not name Summit Road. Nothing on the climb; fill at the ranger station.

  2. Rio Verde – Fountain Hills loop (around the McDowells)

    The loop around the north and east side of the McDowell Mountains.

    • Road
    • 50 mi
    • 2,750 ft up
    • Hard
    • Start: Safeway at DC Ranch, Scottsdale
    • Water: The Safeway at DC Ranch, at the start and finish.
    • Watch: The route page names no hazards. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). That is 50 miles with no water stop on the page, so start at first light and carry all your water.
    Route on RideWithGPSTo the start
    More about Rio Verde – Fountain Hills loop (around the McDowells)

    From the Safeway at DC Ranch it goes up Pima to Dynamite, over the hill to Rio Verde, then left on Saguaro all the way to Shea, per the route page: 50 miles and about 2,750 feet. The page’s note stops at Shea, so check the map for the way back. Saguaro Blvd runs through Fountain Hills past McDowell Mountain Cycles, where the shop’s no-drop road ride (Some Saturdays, 6:30 am) leaves, and past Fountain View Coffee half a mile north of it. You can also start in Fountain Hills: a 48-mile, 2,529-foot RideWithGPS loop through the same three towns starts there. The HonorHealth Tour de Scottsdale (April 10, 2027) runs its 54-mile route around the McDowells through the same three towns.

    Surface: Road. The route page names Pima, Dynamite, Rio Verde, Saguaro and Shea; it does not describe the surface.

    Water: The route page names nothing in between. Fountain View Coffee, 12645 N Saguaro Blvd in Fountain Hills, opens at 6 every day per two listings; call (805) 310-1544 before you count on it.

  3. Gainey (the Scottsdale Cycling loop)

    • Road
    • 29 mi
    • 1,100 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Gainey Village, southeast corner of Scottsdale Rd and Doubletree Ranch Rd, 8977 N Scottsdale Rd, Scottsdale, AZ 85253
    • Watch: The route page names no hazards.

    Ride it with the group: Gainey Thursday (Thursdays, 5:30 am) →

    Route on RideWithGPSTo the start
    More about Gainey (the Scottsdale Cycling loop)

    The route of Scottsdale Cycling’s Gainey ride (Thursdays, 5:30 am), which clips in at the southeast corner of Doubletree and Scottsdale: 29 miles and about 1,100 feet, per the RideWithGPS page. The club’s Strava event names its five hills: Desert Cove, Via Linda, 136th St, 128th St and 124th St. Join the group, or ride the loop on your own any morning.

    Surface: Road. The route page does not describe the surface.

    Watch: The group starts in the dark most of the year, so bring front and rear lights. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). Start at first light and carry all your water.

  4. Usery Loop and Salt River

    East Side Cycling’s RideWithGPS ambassador route through the East Valley’s desert.

    • Road
    • 27 mi
    • 1,500 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Thomas Rd and Power Rd, Mesa (the Walgreens on the corner)
    • Water: The only drinking water on the route is at the top of Usery, near the visitor center, after most of the climbing (East Side Cycling).
    • Watch: Kong is a steep downhill early in the ride.
    Route on RideWithGPSTo the start
    More about Usery Loop and Salt River

    North on Power Rd past Red Mountain, down the steep hill locals call Kong, and along the Salt River. Then up Little Kong, about a mile at 5 to 6 percent, and 4 miles at a steady 5 to 6 percent over Usery Pass. It finishes with a descent to McDowell Rd and a short climb up Hawes through Las Sendas: 27 miles and about 1,500 feet. A side trip goes out to the Cliffs just below Saguaro Lake. The author says people have parked behind the Walgreens at the start; ask first.

    Surface: Paved road. The author says it has a good shoulder for the most part.

    Watch: An older Bikemap route along the Salt River on Bush Highway (about 13 years old) warns that boaters use Bush Highway heavily. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). There is no water until the top of Usery, so start at first light and carry enough for the river and the pass.

  5. Indian Bend Wash path (the Scottsdale Greenbelt)

    An 11-mile path through Scottsdale’s greenbelt of parks, lakes and golf courses (City of Scottsdale).

    • Path
    • 11 mi
    • Easy
    • Start: Chaparral Park, Scottsdale (one of the path’s trailheads)
    • Watch: TrailLink says underpasses take it under almost all road crossings, so expect a few at street level.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about Indian Bend Wash path (the Scottsdale Greenbelt)

    More than 24 underpasses and bridges carry it past the big streets. TrailLink measures 12 miles from Venturoso Park in Phoenix to E Curry Rd in Tempe, with trailheads at Chaparral Park and Eldorado Park in Scottsdale. This is the ride for the evening you land: almost no cross traffic, and you can turn around anywhere. The Bike Lane’s social rides (Some Saturdays, 9:00 am) use the greenbelt and the canals, each ride with its own start.

    Surface: Concrete multiuse path (TrailLink), with more than 24 underpasses and bridges (City of Scottsdale).

    Watch: It is shared with walkers and runners. TrailLink says to watch for flying golf balls where the path passes the tee boxes. Scottsdale’s path rules: keep right and leave the left side for passing. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). Neither the city’s page nor TrailLink names a water fountain.

  6. Indian Bend Wash Greenbelt loop (to Tempe Town Lake)

    • Path
    • 52 mi
    • 1,000 ft up
    • Hard
    • Watch: About 6 miles are on a state road.
    Route on Komoot
    More about Indian Bend Wash Greenbelt loop (to Tempe Town Lake)

    Komoot’s 52-mile loop joins the Indian Bend Wash greenbelt to other paths and roads: past Taliesin West and Camelback Park, down to Tempe Town Lake, and on to a viewpoint over the Salt River. About 1,000 feet of climbing, per Komoot. Much of the way crosses streets on underpasses and overpasses. It is the long day on this list, and most of it is away from cars; it is a loop, so start wherever you are staying along it.

    Surface: Paved throughout. About 32 of the 52 miles are bike path; about 8 are road and about 6 are state road (Komoot).

    Watch: Komoot does not say which. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). It is 52 miles and Komoot names no water stop, so start at first light and plan your refills before you go.

  7. Trail 100 (Charles M. Christiansen Memorial Trail)

    Phoenix’s in-town mountain bike trail runs across the Phoenix Mountains Preserve.

    • Mountain bike
    • 11 mi
    • 850 ft up
    • Moderate
    • Start: Dreamy Draw Park, off SR 51 at Northern Ave
    • Watch: Rocky with loose pebbles (Singletracks).

    Ride it with the group: Night Rider Series @ Trail 100 (Wednesdays, 6:30 pm) →

    Route pageTo the start
    More about Trail 100 (Charles M. Christiansen Memorial Trail)

    MTB Project measures 11.3 miles with 860 feet up, rated intermediate/difficult. Singletracks names the trailheads: Dreamy Draw Park (the main lot), Tatum Blvd at the east end, 7th Ave at the west end, and Mountain View Park. For shorter rides there is MTB Project’s West Side Trail 100 Loop (10.9 miles, 743 feet, from the Central Ave lot in North Mountain Park) and Trailforks’ 5.3-mile intermediate loop on the east side.

    Surface: Singletrack: mild to moderate, with some steep, short climbs (MTB Project). Rocky, with loose pebbles (Singletracks).

    Watch: The west end near the 7th St lot gets a lot of hikers (MTB Project). A Trailforks review says parts of the Fence Line trail on the east loop are hike-a-bike over boulders. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). On Extreme Heat Warning days the city closes the Piestewa Peak Summit Trail and associated trails 8 a.m. to 5 p.m.; that list does not name Trail 100. No page names a place to get water, so carry it all.

  8. McDowell Mountain Competitive Track (Long Loop)

    • Mountain bike
    • 8 mi
    • Moderate
    • Start: Four Peaks Staging Area, McDowell Mountain Regional Park, Fountain Hills
    • Water: Four Peaks Staging Area: water, restrooms with showers, and a bike wash rack (county map).
    • Watch: Ride it one way only.
    Route pageTo the start
    More about McDowell Mountain Competitive Track (Long Loop)

    Maricopa County’s Competitive Track in McDowell Mountain Regional Park, about 14 to 15 miles of trail in all (15 by the county’s web page, 13.7 by its map), has three loops. The 7.9-mile Long Loop is, in the county’s words, designed for the average rider and enjoyed by all skill levels. The 3.0-mile Sport Loop suits intermediate and advanced riders, and the 2.7-mile Technical Loop is for experts only. All three start and finish at the Four Peaks Staging Area. McDowell Mountain Cycles’ night ride (Tuesdays, 7:00 pm) and its Ladies Mountain Bike Ride (Some Mondays, 7:00 am) both leave the Four Peaks lot; the shop rents mountain bikes and delivers them to the park.

    Surface: Mountain bike race track, ridden one way as marked. Don’t ‘improve’ it, per the county.

    Watch: Slower riders yield to faster ones. The Technical Loop is experts only, with steep climbs and technical descents. The county says to carry plenty of water, check conditions, and tell someone your route. Heat, May to October: summer highs average 104 to 106 F (PJAMM). Fill up at Four Peaks before every loop.
